# Benchmark for PSV family functions

## `psv`

```{r}
library(phyr)

# simulate data
nspp = 500
nsite = 100
tree_sim = ape::rtree(n = nspp)
comm_sim = matrix(rbinom(nspp * nsite, size = 1, prob = 0.6), 
                  nrow = nsite, ncol = nspp)
row.names(comm_sim) = paste0("site_", 1:nsite)
colnames(comm_sim) = paste0("t", 1:nspp)
comm_sim = comm_sim[, tree_sim$tip.label]
# about 40 times faster
rbenchmark::benchmark(
  "picante" = {picante::psv(comm_sim, tree_sim)},
  "phyr R" = {phyr::psv(comm_sim, tree_sim, cpp = FALSE)},
  "phyr c++" = {phyr::psv(comm_sim, tree_sim, cpp = TRUE)},
  replications = 10,
  columns = c("test", "replications", "elapsed",
              "relative", "user.self", "sys.self"))
#>       test replications elapsed relative user.self sys.self
#> 3 phyr c++           10   0.339    1.000     0.298    0.030
#> 2   phyr R           10   3.287    9.696     2.907    0.303
#> 1  picante           10  16.265   47.979    14.824    0.795
```

# Benchmark for `pglmm()`

The benchmarks below were run on a MacBook Pro (Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB of memory) with R 4.6.0 and Apple's Accelerate BLAS library, with phyr 1.4.0, lme4 2.0.1, glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 and Matrix 1.7.5; the times and memory of phyr were measured again with phyr 1.9.0 (they changed by less than about 15%, which is within the variation between runs). Each model was fitted once, in a new R session; times are elapsed seconds, and memory is the peak memory of the R session (which uses about 0.3 GB with the packages loaded).

## Simulated data

Community data: `nsp` species (with a coalescent tree) at 20 sites, with 80% of the combinations of species and sites observed, a covariate `x`, and phylogenetic and non-phylogenetic variation among species, variation among sites, and phylogenetic variation of species within sites. The phylogenetic effects are simulated along the tree (Brownian motion), so that large trees do not need the covariance matrix of the species.

```{r}
sim_data <- function(nsp, nsite = 20, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  phy <- ape::rcoal(nsp, tip.label = paste0("sp", 1:nsp))
  h <- max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(phy))
  bm <- function(sd) ape::rTraitCont(phy, sigma = sd / sqrt(h))[phy$tip.label]
  d <- expand.grid(sp = phy$tip.label, site = paste0("s", 1:nsite), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  d <- d[sort(sample(nrow(d), round(0.8 * nrow(d)))), ]
  i <- match(d$sp, phy$tip.label)
  j <- match(d$site, paste0("s", 1:nsite))
  u_phy <- bm(0.5)
  u_sp <- rnorm(nsp, sd = 0.3)
  u_site <- rnorm(nsite, sd = 0.5)
  u_nested <- sapply(1:nsite, function(k) bm(0.3)) # one column per site
  d$x <- rnorm(nrow(d))
  eta <- 0.3 * d$x + u_phy[i] + u_sp[i] + u_site[j] + u_nested[cbind(i, j)]
  d$y <- eta + rnorm(nrow(d))
  d$pa <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta - 0.5))
  d$count <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(eta - 0.5))
  list(d = d, phy = phy)
}
```

## Comparison with lme4 and glmmTMB

Models without phylogeny, `(1 | sp) + (1 | site)`, fitted by maximum likelihood with `pglmm()`, `lme4::lmer()` and `lme4::glmer()`, and `glmmTMB()`:

```{r}
s <- sim_data(5000)
d <- s$d
pglmm(pa ~ x + (1 | sp) + (1 | site), data = d, family = "binomial", REML = FALSE,
      add.obs.re = FALSE)
lme4::glmer(pa ~ x + (1 | sp) + (1 | site), data = d, family = "binomial")
glmmTMB::glmmTMB(pa ~ x + (1 | sp) + (1 | site), data = d, family = "binomial")
```

| Species | Observations | Family | phyr | lme4 | glmmTMB |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1000 | 16,000 | gaussian | 0.14 | 0.62 | 1.71 |
| 1000 | 16,000 | binomial | 0.55 | 1.68 | 1.79 |
| 1000 | 16,000 | poisson | 0.49 | 1.60 | 1.63 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | gaussian | 0.17 | 0.72 | 2.39 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | binomial | 0.88 | 3.33 | 2.58 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | poisson | 0.91 | 2.77 | 2.22 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | gaussian | 0.60 | 1.16 | 4.94 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | binomial | 2.36 | 8.44 | 5.04 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | poisson | 2.34 | 9.43 | 5.04 |

Time (seconds). With 5000 species, the R sessions used 0.6 to 0.7 GB of memory with phyr and lme4, and 1.0 to 1.2 GB with glmmTMB. The three packages give the same estimates: the log-likelihoods of phyr and glmmTMB agree to 1e-7, their slopes to 1e-6 and the standard errors of the slopes to 2e-5 (relative); lme4 stops slightly earlier for binomial and poisson models (log-likelihoods lower by up to 1e-3), and its standard errors of the slopes of these models are up to 1.6% smaller (they are computed differently).

Models with a phylogenetic term, `(1 | sp__) + (1 | site)` in phyr, which is `(1 | sp) + propto(0 + sp | g, C) + (1 | site)` in glmmTMB (with `g` a factor with one level and `C` the phylogenetic covariance matrix); lme4 cannot fit phylogenetic terms:

```{r}
s <- sim_data(5000)
d <- s$d
pglmm(pa ~ x + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site), data = d, family = "binomial",
      cov_ranef = list(sp = s$phy), REML = FALSE, add.obs.re = FALSE)
d$spf <- factor(d$sp, levels = s$phy$tip.label)
d$g <- factor(1)
C <- ape::vcv(s$phy)
glmmTMB::glmmTMB(pa ~ x + (1 | spf) + propto(0 + spf | g, C) + (1 | site),
                 data = d, family = "binomial")
```

| Species | Observations | Family | phyr | glmmTMB | phyr memory (GB) | glmmTMB memory (GB) |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 300 | 4,800 | gaussian | 0.12 | 1.87 | 0.4 | 0.6 |
| 300 | 4,800 | binomial | 0.35 | 2.06 | 0.4 | 0.5 |
| 300 | 4,800 | poisson | 0.39 | 1.77 | 0.4 | 0.6 |
| 1000 | 16,000 | gaussian | 0.36 | 12.2 | 0.4 | 2.1 |
| 1000 | 16,000 | binomial | 1.43 | 11.3 | 0.4 | 2.1 |
| 1000 | 16,000 | poisson | 1.27 | 12.0 | 0.4 | 2.1 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | gaussian | 0.56 | 73.8 | 0.5 | 7.4 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | binomial | 3.12 | 66.2 | 0.5 | 7.1 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | poisson | 3.02 | 63.0 | 0.5 | 7.2 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | gaussian | 1.51 | 703 | 0.7 | 13.0 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | binomial | 7.25 | 671 | 0.9 | 12.5 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | poisson | 7.80 | 708 | 0.9 | 11.7 |

Time (seconds) and memory. glmmTMB works with the dense covariance matrix of the species, so its time and memory grow much faster than the number of species, while phyr uses the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (`sparse = TRUE`, the default): with 5000 species, phyr is 90 to 470 times faster, with less than a tenth of the memory. The estimates are the same: log-likelihoods within 4e-7, slopes within 3e-6, and standard errors within 5e-5 (relative).

## Large phylogenies

The full model of the simulated data, `y ~ x + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site)`, with the defaults of `pglmm()` (REML, the Laplace approximation for binomial and poisson models, and the sparse code):

```{r}
s <- sim_data(10000)
pglmm(pa ~ x + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site), data = s$d,
      family = "binomial", cov_ranef = list(sp = s$phy))
```

| Species | Observations | gaussian | binomial | poisson | Memory (GB) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1000 | 16,000 | 5.7 | 8.7 | 11.5 | 0.6 |
| 2000 | 32,000 | 5.8 | 16.3 | 27.4 | 0.8 to 1.0 |
| 5000 | 80,000 | 14.6 | 50.8 | 64.7 | 1.5 to 1.8 |
| 10000 | 160,000 | 31.2 | 76.8 | 149.4 | 2.4 to 3.4 |

Time (seconds) and memory: time and memory grow about linearly with the number of species. The nested term `(1 | sp__@site)` (the phylogeny of the species within each site) is the most costly: without it, the models with 5000 species of the previous section took 1.5 to 8 seconds (fitted by maximum likelihood).

## Dense and sparse code, and earlier versions of phyr

The same full model, fitted with the sparse code (the default), with the dense code (`sparse = FALSE`, the covariance matrices of the species), and with phyr 1.1.3 (the dense code, and penalized quasi-likelihood for binomial models):

| Species | Observations | gaussian, 1.1.3 | gaussian, dense | gaussian, sparse | binomial PQL, 1.1.3 | binomial PQL, sparse | binomial Laplace, sparse |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 | 800 | 16.6 | 0.36 | 0.14 | 30.2 | 0.18 | 0.23 |
| 100 | 1,600 | 139 | 2.2 | 0.44 | 313 | 0.42 | 0.45 |
| 200 | 3,200 | > 900 | 16.3 | 0.70 | > 900 | 1.2 | 1.5 |
| 400 | 6,400 |  | 100 | 1.8 |  | 2.7 | 4.0 |
| 1000 | 16,000 |  | 742 | 5.7 |  | 4.8 | 8.7 |

Time (seconds; phyr 1.1.3 was stopped after 900 seconds). The dense code needed 3.3 GB of memory with 400 species and 9.3 GB with 1000 species, the sparse code 0.4 and 0.6 GB. With up to 400 species, the estimates of phyr 1.1.3 and 1.4.0, and of the dense and sparse code, are the same within the tolerances of the optimizers (variances within 0.006, slopes within 2e-4). With 1000 species, the optimizer of the dense code (L-BFGS) failed after one iteration, with a warning, and the dense fit is 668 units of log-likelihood below the sparse one: use the sparse code (the default) for large models.

# Why phylogenetic random terms matter: a simulation study

When related species respond alike, the species are not independent replicates. These simulations compare `pglmm()` with the phylogenetic term (PGLMM), the same model without the phylogeny (GLMM, `(1 | sp)` instead of `(1 | sp__)`) and a GLM without random terms, on data simulated with phylogenetic signal.

Design: 100 species (a coalescent tree of height one) at 15 sites (1500 observations), gaussian, binary and poisson responses, and two questions:

- **Trait**: the effect of a species trait `x`, simulated by Brownian motion (so it has phylogenetic signal), with species effects that have a phylogenetic part (variance 1) and an independent part (variance 0.25), and site effects (variance 0.25).
- **Trait x environment**: the interaction of the trait with an environmental variable `e` of the sites, with, in addition, phylogenetic species slopes on `e` (variance 0.5).

Each case was simulated 500 times with a true slope of zero (type I error, coverage of the 95% confidence intervals) and 500 times with a slope of 0.3 (power), and fitted with the defaults of `pglmm()` (REML, Laplace approximation, Wald tests):

```{r}
sim_one <- function(seed, family, scenario, beta, nsp = 100, nsite = 15, phylo = TRUE) {
  set.seed(seed)
  phy <- ape::rcoal(nsp, tip.label = paste0("sp", 1:nsp))
  phy$edge.length <- phy$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(phy))
  L <- t(chol(ape::vcv(phy)))
  trait <- as.numeric(L %*% rnorm(nsp))
  trait <- (trait - mean(trait)) / sd(trait)
  env <- rnorm(nsite)
  d <- expand.grid(sp = phy$tip.label, site = paste0("s", 1:nsite), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  i <- match(d$sp, phy$tip.label)
  k <- match(d$site, paste0("s", 1:nsite))
  d$x <- trait[i]
  d$e <- env[k]
  Lu <- if (phylo) L else diag(nsp) # without signal: independent species effects
  u <- as.numeric(Lu %*% rnorm(nsp)) + rnorm(nsp, sd = 0.5)
  v <- rnorm(nsite, sd = 0.5)
  if (scenario == "trait") {
    eta <- beta * d$x + u[i] + v[k]
    f <- list(PGLMM = y ~ x + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site), GLMM = y ~ x + (1 | sp) + (1 | site))
  } else {
    w <- sqrt(0.5) * as.numeric(Lu %*% rnorm(nsp))
    eta <- 0.3 * d$e + beta * d$x * d$e + u[i] + v[k] + w[i] * d$e
    f <- list(PGLMM = y ~ x * e + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (e | sp__),
              GLMM = y ~ x * e + (1 | sp) + (1 | site) + (e | sp))
  }
  d$y <- switch(family, gaussian = eta + rnorm(nrow(d)),
                binomial = rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta)), poisson = rpois(nrow(d), exp(eta)))
  lapply(f, function(fo) pglmm(fo, data = d, family = family, cov_ranef = list(sp = phy)))
}
```

With phylogenetic signal (true slope zero, except the last column):

| Scenario | Family | Type I error: PGLMM | GLMM | GLM | 95% CI coverage: PGLMM | GLMM | GLM | RMSE: PGLMM | GLMM | Power (slope 0.3): PGLMM |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Trait | gaussian | 6.4% | 61.4% | 81.8% | 93.6% | 38.6% | 18.2% | 0.18 | 0.37 | 52.4% |
| Trait | binomial | 8.6% | 58.2% | 70.8% | 91.4% | 41.8% | 29.2% | 0.22 | 0.37 | 38.8% |
| Trait | poisson | 7.2% | 61.4% | 87.8% | 92.8% | 38.6% | 12.2% | 0.18 | 0.37 | 49.6% |
| Trait x environment | gaussian | 7.4% | 66.0% | 72.2% | 92.6% | 34.0% | 27.8% | 0.11 | 0.27 | 82.0% |
| Trait x environment | binomial | 9.8% | 49.8% | 54.8% | 90.2% | 50.2% | 45.2% | 0.17 | 0.27 | 55.4% |
| Trait x environment | poisson | 6.8% | 67.4% | 81.2% | 93.2% | 32.6% | 18.8% | 0.11 | 0.27 | 85.2% |

Without the phylogenetic term, the standard errors were only 19% to 30% of the standard deviations of the estimates across data sets (6% to 27% for the GLM), as the model treats the 100 related species as independent; with it, 87% to 95%. Thus, without the phylogeny, a true null hypothesis was rejected in half or more of the data sets. With it, the estimates were also about twice as accurate (root mean squared error). (The GLMM rejects more often when the slope is 0.3 too, but this is no gain in power, as it also does when the slope is zero.)

Without phylogenetic signal (the same design, with independent species effects of the same variances, and a true slope of zero), the phylogenetic term costs little: the type I errors of PGLMM and GLMM were both close to or below 5%, and the RMSE of PGLMM was 8% to 21% larger (the phylogenetic variance, estimated above zero by chance, competes with the trait, which still has phylogenetic signal):

| Scenario | Family | Type I error: PGLMM | GLMM | GLM | RMSE: PGLMM | GLMM |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Trait | gaussian | 3.0% | 3.6% | 48.0% | 0.126 | 0.108 |
| Trait | binomial | 3.0% | 3.4% | 29.0% | 0.135 | 0.116 |
| Trait | poisson | 2.8% | 3.4% | 79.2% | 0.118 | 0.107 |
| Trait x environment | gaussian | 6.4% | 7.2% | 23.4% | 0.087 | 0.081 |
| Trait x environment | binomial | 3.6% | 4.0% | 11.4% | 0.108 | 0.089 |
| Trait x environment | poisson | 5.0% | 5.4% | 79.2% | 0.085 | 0.077 |

## Tests for binary data

With binary data and phylogenetic signal, the Wald test of PGLMM rejected a true null hypothesis somewhat too often (8.6% and 9.8% above). Tests from maximum likelihood fits did worse, as maximum likelihood underestimates the phylogenetic variances when there are effectively few independent species: in the same 500 data sets of each scenario, the Wald test of the ML fits rejected it in 14.2% (trait) and 16.2% (trait x environment) of the data sets, and the likelihood ratio test of `anova()` (from ML fits) in 10.6% and 11.2%. The parametric bootstrap test of `pglmm_boot_LRT()` does not rely on the chi-square approximation; with 199 simulations per test, in 100 data sets of the trait scenario, it rejected the true null hypothesis in 4% of them (the Wald and chi-square tests in 8% and 9% of the same data sets):

```{r}
m <- sim_one(1, "binomial", "trait", beta = 0)
m0 <- update(m$PGLMM, . ~ . - x)
pglmm_boot_LRT(m$PGLMM, m0, nsim = 199, ncores = 8)
```

# Benchmark for `phylo_signal()`

`phylo_signal()` estimates Pagel's lambda or Blomberg's K of a trait, optionally with known standard errors of the species means. It is compared here with `phytools::phylosig()`, `geiger::fitContinuous()`, `phylosignal::phyloSignal()`, `picante::phylosignal()`, `phylolm::phylolm()`, `caper::pgls()` and `nlme::gls()` with `ape::corPagel()`. Only phytools and geiger also fit lambda with known standard errors (`phylolm(..., measurement_error = TRUE)` estimates an unknown error variance instead, a different model), and only phytools fits K with them.

The benchmarks were run on the same computer as those of `pglmm()` (Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB, R 4.6.0 with Accelerate BLAS), with phytools 2.5.2, geiger 2.0.12, phylosignal 1.3.1, picante 1.8.4, phylolm 2.6.5, caper 1.0.4 and nlme 3.1.172, on one core.

## Simulated data

A coalescent tree, a trait that evolved by Brownian motion along the tree with its branches transformed by Pagel's lambda, and, for the fits with measurement error, standard errors between 0.05 and 0.6 with the corresponding noise added to the trait:

```{r}
sim_trait <- function(n, lambda, se = TRUE, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  phy <- ape::rcoal(n)
  tl <- phylolm::transf.branch.lengths(phy, "lambda", parameters = list(lambda = lambda))$tree
  x <- ape::rTraitCont(tl, sigma = 1)[phy$tip.label]
  s <- NULL
  if (se) {
    s <- setNames(runif(n, 0.05, 0.6), phy$tip.label)
    x <- x + rnorm(n, 0, s)
  }
  list(phy = phy, x = x, se = s,
       data = data.frame(sp = phy$tip.label, x = unname(x), row.names = phy$tip.label))
}
d <- sim_trait(1000, lambda = 0.6)
```

## Pagel's lambda

The same model fitted with each package (without `se` for the packages that do not take it):

```{r}
phylo_signal(x, d$phy, se = se, data = cbind(d$data, se = d$se), species = sp)
phytools::phylosig(d$phy, d$x, method = "lambda", se = d$se)
geiger::fitContinuous(d$phy, d$x, SE = d$se, model = "lambda")
phylosignal::phyloSignal(phylobase::phylo4d(d$phy, tip.data = d$data["x"]), methods = "Lambda")
phylolm::phylolm(x ~ 1, data = d$data, phy = d$phy, model = "lambda")
caper::pgls(x ~ 1, caper::comparative.data(d$phy, d$data, "sp"), lambda = "ML")
nlme::gls(x ~ 1, data = d$data, method = "ML",
          correlation = ape::corPagel(0.5, d$phy, form = ~sp, fixed = FALSE))
```

| Species | phyr | phyr, `se` | geiger | geiger, `se` | phylolm | phylosignal | nlme | phytools | phytools, `se` | caper |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1000 | < 0.01 | 0.03 | 1.5 | 1.1 | 0.07 | 1.5 | 4.7 | 5.2 | 113 | 63 |
| 2000 | < 0.01 | 0.05 | 2.2 | 1.7 | 0.14 | 10.5 | 36 | 34 | 533 | 241 |
| 5000 | 0.01 | 0.11 | 4.5 | 4.2 | 0.41 | 273 | 683 | 342 | | |
| 20000 | 0.02 | 0.36 | 15.9 | 15.2 | 1.39 | | | | | |

Time (seconds) for one fit, without tests; empty cells were not run, as the previous size took more than two minutes. phyr, geiger and phylolm compute the likelihood in time linear in the number of species (without the covariance matrix of the species); the other packages use the dense covariance matrix, and their time grows with its cube.

To compare the estimates, the lambda of each package is scored on the same profile log-likelihood (the likelihood of the model maximized over the variance and the mean, at that lambda), the one all packages maximize:

```{r}
prof_loglik <- function(lambda, x, phy, se = NULL) {
  C <- ape::vcv(phy)[names(x), names(x)]
  Cl <- lambda * C + (1 - lambda) * diag(diag(C))
  M <- if (is.null(se)) 0 else diag(se[names(x)]^2)
  ll <- function(log_sig2) {
    V <- exp(log_sig2) * Cl + M
    iV <- solve(V)
    a <- sum(iV %*% x) / sum(iV)
    r <- x - a
    -0.5 * (sum(r * (iV %*% r)) + determinant(V)$modulus + length(x) * log(2 * pi))
  }
  optimise(ll, c(-20, 10), maximum = TRUE)$objective
}
```

Across 80 simulated data sets (lambda of 0, 0.3, 0.7 and 1, 10 data sets each, with 100 and 300 species), the number of data sets where the estimate of each package is below the maximum (the log-likelihood of phyr's estimate) by more than 0.001 and by more than 1:

| Without measurement error | phyr | geiger | phylolm | caper | phytools | phylosignal | nlme |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Failed | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 13 |
| Below by > 0.001 | 0 | 12 | 21 | 21 | 32 | 33 | 4 |
| Below by > 1 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 10 | 10 | 4 |
| Largest difference | 0 | 3.1 | 3.1 | 3.1 | 5.9 | 5.6 | |
| Median time, 300 species (s) | 0.001 | 0.88 | 0.02 | 3.5 | 0.36 | 0.09 | 0.45 |

The estimates agree on average, and most differences are in data sets with lambda = 1, where the maximum can be slightly above 1: lambda can be as large as the height of the tree over the height of its deepest internal node (for these trees, about 1.00002), and without measurement error the likelihood rises steeply in that narrow interval. geiger, phylolm and caper keep lambda below 1; phytools and phylosignal search up to the maximum with one call to `optimize()`, whose precision (about 1e-4) is coarser than the interval. phylolm and caper also stopped at their lower bound (lambda of 1e-7) in one data set whose estimate is 0.16. nlme did not converge in 13 data sets, and does not bound lambda: it returned values below 0 or above the maximum in 4 others (where the covariance matrix is not valid).

| With measurement error | phyr | geiger | phytools |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Below by > 0.001 | 0 | 5 | 7 |
| Below by > 1 | 0 | 0 | 7 |
| Largest difference | 0 | 0.04 | 101 |
| Mean lambda, true lambda 0 (300 species) | 0.001 | 0.001 | 0.100 |
| Mean lambda, true lambda 0.3 (300 species) | 0.265 | 0.265 | 0.470 |
| Median time, 300 species (s) | 0.012 | 0.76 | 10 |

With measurement error, phytools stopped at a local maximum near lambda = 1 in 7 of the 80 data sets (37 to 101 units of log-likelihood below the maximum), which also changes its test of lambda = 0 from P of about 1 to P of about 0, and biases its mean estimate upwards. The small differences of geiger are data sets whose maximum is above 1. `phylo_signal()` evaluates the profile likelihood on a grid of lambda between 0 and the maximum before refining the best value, so it does not depend on starting values.

## Blomberg's K

```{r}
d <- sim_trait(2000, lambda = 0.8, se = FALSE)
phylo_signal(d$x, d$phy, method = "K", nsim = 999)
phytools::phylosig(d$phy, d$x, method = "K", test = TRUE, nsim = 999)
picante::phylosignal(d$x[d$phy$tip.label], d$phy, reps = 999)
phylosignal::phyloSignal(phylobase::phylo4d(d$phy, tip.data = d$data["x"]),
                         methods = "K", reps = 999)
```

| Species | phyr | phylosignal | picante | phytools |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | 0.03 | 0.18 | 0.39 | 1.1 |
| 1000 | 0.06 | 0.75 | 1.9 | 4.3 |
| 2000 | 0.11 | 4.5 | 14.8 | 18.5 |

Time (seconds) for K and its randomization test with 999 randomizations, without measurement error. The four packages give the same K (to 8 significant digits), and P-values that agree within the error of the randomizations. With measurement error (`se`), K and its test took 0.19 seconds with phyr and 36 seconds with phytools for 300 species (the same K), and 0.43 and 2.2 seconds with phyr for 1000 and 5000 species.

# Benchmark for `cor_phylo()`

```{r}
library(ape)
# Set up parameter values for simulating data
n <- 50
phy <- rcoal(n, tip.label = 1:n)
trt_names <- paste0("par", 1:2)

R <- matrix(c(1, 0.7, 0.7, 1), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
d <- c(0.3, 0.95)
B2 <- 1

Se <- c(0.2, 1)
M <- matrix(Se, nrow = n, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(M) <- trt_names

# Set up needed matrices for the simulations
p <- length(d)

star <- stree(n)
star$edge.length <- array(1, dim = c(n, 1))
star$tip.label <- phy$tip.label

Vphy <- vcv(phy)
Vphy <- Vphy/max(Vphy)
Vphy <- Vphy/exp(determinant(Vphy)$modulus[1]/n)

tau <- matrix(1, nrow = n, ncol = 1) %*% diag(Vphy) - Vphy
C <- matrix(0, nrow = p * n, ncol = p * n)
for (i in 1:p) for (j in 1:p) {
  Cd <- (d[i]^tau * (d[j]^t(tau)) * (1 - (d[i] * d[j])^Vphy))/(1 - d[i] * d[j])
  C[(n * (i - 1) + 1):(i * n), (n * (j - 1) + 1):(j * n)] <- R[i, j] * Cd
}
MM <- matrix(M^2, ncol = 1)
V <- C + diag(as.numeric(MM))

iD <- t(chol(V))

XX <- iD %*% rnorm(2 * n)
X <- matrix(XX, n, p)
colnames(X) <- trt_names
rownames(X) <- phy$tip.label
rownames(M) <- phy$tip.label

U <- list(cbind(rnorm(n, mean = 2, sd = 10)))
names(U) <- trt_names[2]

X[,2] <- X[,2] + B2[1] * U[[1]][,1] - B2[1] * mean(U[[1]][,1])

z <- cor_phylo(variates = X,
               covariates = U,
               meas_errors = M,
               phy = phy,
               species = phy$tip.label)


U2 <- list(NULL, matrix(rnorm(n, mean = 2, sd = 10), nrow = n, ncol = 1))
rownames(U2[[2]]) <- phy$tip.label
colnames(U2[[2]]) <- "par2"
X2 = X
X2[,2] <- X2[,2] + B2[1] * U2[[2]][,1] - B2[1] * mean(U2[[2]][,1])

z_r <- corphylo(X = X2, SeM = M, U = U2, phy = phy, method = "Nelder-Mead")

rbenchmark::benchmark(
  "cor_phylo" = {cor_phylo(variates = X, covariates = U, meas_errors = M,
                           phy = phy, species = phy$tip.label)},
  "corphylo" = {corphylo(X = X2, SeM = M, U = U2, phy = phy, method = "Nelder-Mead")},
  replications = 5,
  columns = c("test", "replications", "elapsed",
              "relative", "user.self", "sys.self")
)
#>        test replications elapsed relative user.self sys.self
#> 1 cor_phylo            5   4.511    1.000     4.329    0.062
#> 2  corphylo            5  16.190    3.589    13.863    1.369
```
